Gaf

Just going back a few years, turophile asked: “What is a gaf anyway?”

In Ireland, or in Dublin certainly, a ‘gaf’ is a slang word commonly used for a house. But its usually only used among young people. I’ve not heard it used among older people so it could be a relatively common word. In which case, the typo in question would be in the book.

Just rediscovering this tune having heard a marvelous version on Marcus Hernon’s “Traditional Irish Music played on Concert Flute.” On this track, its a whistle solo. I prefer it with just 2 parts like Marcus plays it.

↳ Posted by Paahto on July 19th, 2009.

Gaf

Is also a type of rigging on a sailboat, and probably can refer to a boat in its entirety. Just to make it more confusing.

↳ Posted by wormdiet on August 18th, 2009.

Make the “gaffe”

↳ Posted by wormdiet on August 18th, 2009.

According to the OED, the earliest recorded use of the word ‘gaff’ for a house is 1932. The word was used in the 18th century (1753) to mean a fair and was extended to mean “any public place of amusement” (theatre for example).

Gaf, gaff and gaffe

… and again going back a few years, a far as I know there is no such word as “gaf”. “Gaff” for a house and “gaffe” for a mistake appear to come from the same word originally. But I’m pretty sure they’re separate words now.

I just looked them up in the OED and they weren’t there in quite the same way we use them now, but I have a 35 year old edition (roughly) so maybe they’d be in there now.

↳ Posted by ethical blend on October 26th, 2012.

From Paddy O’Brien’s notes to his tune collection (don’t know if this has been posted elsewhere):

[Before the founding of the Gaelic Athletic Association (G.A.A.) in 1884, hurling was played openly in fields and byways. The boy in the gap was the goalkeeper or the last defender in a game where one parish would take on a rival parish. If the ball went past him, his job was to retrieve it and whack it as far as possible into the territory of the opposing team, which might number more than a hundred. These sports contests more often than not turned into ferocious faction fights.]

The Boy In The Gap, X:7

This is Paddy O’Brien’s way of playing this reel. It is from his first tune collection, tape #1.
It is similar to the setting posted by slainte, but has C# (mostly) in the second and third parts
and the phrasing of the first part is different (decB instead of dedc). Getting to the c sooner seems to
move it along, also, the end of the third part differs from all the other settings here (and I like it very much).

The Boy In The Gap, X:14

I’m not sure whether yet another setting is a useful thing, but X:14 was my attempt to catch the flavour of the tune as I learnt it some years ago from a recording by Micho Russell, where it is played in two versions with ‘John in the Fog’ in between. The chords are my addition, so use or ignore ad lib.

I remember seeing MR in a whistle competition at a Fleadh in Listowel in the late ’70s. He came third in the over-18s.

↳ Posted by Bazza on April 30th, 2026.

Re: The Boy In The Gap

In O’Neill’s this is called the Boys of Cappoquin. In Ryan’s Mammoth Collection we find the Boys in the Gap title. The Chief has been found to have taken a handful of tunes from that book and Hibernisized the titles - i.e., The Green Branch becomes the Reconciliation; Bernardo’s Hornpipe becomes The Humours of Castle Bernard. This seems to be one instance where his attempt at a more Irish title didn’t take.

In Canon Goodman’s collection it’s The Farmer’s Lass. The earliest recorded version is Morrison/McKenna’s 1929 disc, I believe. Leo Rowsome called it Conroy’s Reel on a 1940s disc, in tribute to a piping colleague.

The Traditional Tune Archive also has this to say: “The ‘boy/gap’ title holds sexual connotations for some.” The first musician I met up with was a piper who told me much the same story - this title, and The Boy in the Boat, were lewd references to, erm, well, you know…;) Or whatever emoticon…;)
